newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FOCUS-Rebel raid highlights stalemate in Sri Lanka war.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rebel raid highlights stalemate in Sri Lanka war.

text.p: Last week's fierce Tamil rebel raid on Sri Lanka's army has demolished government claims the guerrillas are a spent force and that peace was at hand, political analysts said on Sunday.

The raid on the northern crossroad town of Paranthan, which forced army gunners to destroy several artillery pieces to prevent them from falling into rebel hands, shows guerrilla chief Velupillai Prabhakaran retains a formidable military machine, analysts said.
"Prabhakaran is far from being a spent force," political analyst Dayan Jayatilleka told Reuters. "He can pick the time and place, concentrate his forces and punch through."
The government said 350 Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels died in Thursday's attack on the Paranthan army base, and said it lost at least 161 soldiers.
The rebels admitted the loss of 140 fighters, including 78 women, and said they destroyed nine 122mm and two 130mm guns, some of the army's most powerful guns.
"The LTTE seems determined not to allow the government to talk from a position of strength," said one senior military officer in the north, who declined to be identified.

The government's two-pronged strategy of trying to force the rebels back for talks while offering autonomy to woo Tamils away from the Tigers' demand for independence, will not work as long as the LTTE remains militarily powerful, the military officer said.

The military has been unable to successfully wage the war, now in its 14th year, because of inadequate manpower and equipment, poor morale, weak leadership and a lack of clear political direction, the officer added.

President Chandrika Kumaratunga last year unveiled a peace plan offering extensive autonomy to minority Tamils as an alternative to the separate state the Tigers are fighting for in the north and east of the mainly Sinhalese Indian Ocean island.
But it has been stalled in parliament because of bickering with the main opposition United National Party, whose support Kumaratunga needs to get the two-thirds majority required to pass the plan.

Although Kumaratunga has repeatedly said the war will be over in just one year, her military campaign got bogged down after the euphoria generated by the capture of Jaffna, the Tigers' northern stronghold, in December 1995.
"The LTTE wants to show that one year after the army took Jaffna the northern theatre has not yet been pacified," said Jayatilleka.
"The government doesn't understand the mentality of guerrillas. For Prabhakaran, this war is a protracted one. With every such attack he gets worldwide attention."
The loss of artillery also means the government will be unable to cut defence spending as much as it had hoped for this year, he added.
"Part of Prabhakaran's strategy is to weaken the economy and make the cost of the war unbearable for the government," former army chief Lt. General Dennis Perera told Reuters.

The government has said it plans to cut defence spending to 44 billion rupees ($772 million) this year since it had bought most of its arms in calendar 1996, when war spending was almost 50 billion rupees ($877 million).
Other analysts, however, felt the upturn expected in the economy this year could cushion the impact of higher defence spending.

"These are temporary setbacks, which will be offset by the general economic turnaround that is expected this year," said Sanjeeva Gunawardena, manager for institutional sales at Commercial Stock Brokers.
"The stock market was not disturbed by the news," he added. "This type of attack and the losses are factored in when investors plan their investment strategy."
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the war. The LTTE says the toll is much higher.
